Par FaceTime, Hannah me fait faire le to: Over FaceTime, Hannah gives me a tour of her living room. She wants to show me her decorations for the month of Ramadan. “I bought some lights and we made banners. I wanted to create a festive atmosphere for Adam, especially since we’re alone here…,” she explains. In these times of lockdown, Hannah and her son won’t be able to count on the warmth of the community to fill the loneliness. “Normally, we would go at least twice a week to share community meals at the mosque. It was good for morale, and it helped the budget…,” she says. Hannah is one of thousands of people in Quebec who value the month of Ramadan for the material support it offers, but above all for the community support. The pandemic and lockdown will certainly upend this annual tradition.
« C’est pas grave, ce sera un ramadan di: “It’s okay, it’ll be a different Ramadan, but we’ll find the positive in it,” the mother concludes. Behind her, the lights twinkle. ***Foudil Selmoune is an imam at the ICC mosque in Brossard. Every year, in normal times, his mosque welcomes and feeds some 300 people free of charge each evening of Ramadan. In the last days of the month, that number rises to 1,000. “This year, obviously, that won’t be possible. So we decided to prepare hot takeout meals for the breaking of the fast. That way, God willing, we’ll be able to prepare meals for 300 people every day of Ramadan,” he explains. He points out that, normally, the people who come to share meals at the mosque don’t necessarily do so out of financial need, but mainly for the spiritual and community side of it. With that in mind, the takeout meals are being offered to everyone during the lockdown. “We even put up a sign outside, ‘Free meals for everyone,’ to share these blessings with our neighbours and our wider community.” Still, most of the people who contact the mosque for meals during this unique Ramadan are often in precarious situations: students, single mothers and others. “If someone can’t come to pick up the meal, we have volunteers who deliver it. I do it myself when I can,” says Imam Selmoune.
Au bout du fil, Sister Sabria rigole. «: On the other end of the line, Sister Sabria laughs. “Yes, it’s different this year. We have to wash the food three times and take even more sanitary measures, it’s exhausting!” says the 72-year-old. Sister Sabria has become her only name. An icon of the Muslim community, she has fed thousands of people for decades, standing at the stove herself. After stopping last year because of health problems, she has put her apron back on in these troubled times. “I had a dream. I felt that I had to get back to it, to help…”
Normalement, Sister Sabria et son armée: Normally, Sister Sabria and her army of volunteers feed some 700 people each night of Ramadan, on top of her regular job. This year, confined to her apartment, she will make do with 20 people, most of them homeless people and students. “That’s pretty much the most I can manage on my own in my kitchen,” she laments. At the same time, her foundation has set up a food basket project. “I really try to personalize the baskets. I call each family and ask about their needs and tastes. I also have to prioritize by urgency, there’s too much demand, and I take people’s donations very seriously…,” she explains.
Il faut savoir que pendant le ramadan, c: It’s worth knowing that during Ramadan, every Muslim is required to feed at least one person in need over the course of the month. This obligatory charity goes by the name Zakat al-Fitr, and many Montrealers entrust their money to Sister Sabria. As needs grow, help fortunately follows. When I called her on a Saturday morning, Nermine Barbouch was in the middle of work. Nermine Barbouch is a liaison officer and spokesperson for Centre Amal, an organization that provides psychosocial services to vulnerable women and families, while also carrying out awareness activities on domestic violence and mental health in ethnocultural communities. Alongside remote psychosocial follow-up for its clients during the lockdown, the centre has launched a virtual food basket initiative in the form of grocery gift cards. “I expected to feed about ten families, but we’re now at more than sixty, on top of the donations. The community has been extremely generous,” says Nermine Barbouch. The liaison officer doesn’t attribute this generosity solely to the influence of the month of Ramadan, but to the pandemic. “COVID has doubled people’s generosity. The pandemic has touched all of us, rich or poor, it has awakened consciences. People want to help.”
C’est cette envie d’aider qui a motivé F: It’s this desire to help that motivated Fekhreddin Chibani to start a small foundation, Change Dounia (Dounia means “world” in Arabic). “I don’t even have the ambition of making it a foundation. You can just call it a group of young people who want to take action,” says the engineer by training. Initially motivated by a wish to help the most disadvantaged in his country of origin, Algeria, Fekhreddin Chibani quickly realized that the needs were enormous, and everywhere in the world. Including the city where he grew up, Montréal. “Last year, we organized an iftar (the meal to break the fast) for international students here. They were alone, isolated. Ramadan is a great opportunity to come closer together and show solidarity,” he says. With the pandemic, that plan obviously fell through this year. “We thought we could prepare hot meals and bring them to them, but the logistics were complicated and would have meant a lot of back and forth, not ideal with social distancing!” The solution: Ramadan baskets delivered to people’s homes, with enough fresh and non-perishable food to last a week. What started out as a way to help international students turned into a community initiative. “We started getting requests from refugee families, or people in need. And not only Muslims. You don’t refuse to help your neighbour,” continues the founder of Change Dounia. Thanks to the generosity of a butcher shop and a fruit and vegetable store, which donated their products, 150 baskets have already been distributed. “We’re doing our best, but I get hundreds of messages a day. At some point, I’m not Trudeau either!” he jokes. Like his elder Sister Sabria, Fekhreddin makes sure his baskets meet real food needs and tastes. “You’ll find honey, semolina, couscous, coriander, Middle Eastern spices. Everything you need to eat what you like to eat, not just enough to survive.”
Pour lui, en effet, il est important de: For him, it is indeed important to preserve the dignity of the people being given to, in both substance and form. “When we deliver, people should think it’s just a regular delivery from Maxi,” he says. As for what’s in the baskets, his example is all the more telling. “The basket you receive, we want it to be the one your mother would have given you. We want to fill not only your stomach, but your eyes and your heart.”
